'''4.''' To shed one’s blood; be severely wounded or die, as in battle or the like.
{{smaller block|Cæsar must ''bleed'' for it.

'''5.''' To lose sap, gum, or juice, as a tree or a vine.

{{smaller block|The defects in the plates, whose presence may not even be suspected, become exposed, and being attacked anew by the acids in the water used for washing out the boiler, which are not neutralized by the soda, are caused to ''bleed''.

{{smaller block|A decaying pine of stately size ''bleeding'' amber.
{{right|''Miller.''}}}}
'''3.''' To extort or exact money from; sponge on: as, the sharpers ''bled'' him freely. [Slang.]

'''bleeder''' (blē′dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who lets blood.—'''2.''' A person who is naturally predisposed to bleed. See ''hemophilia.''

'''bleed-hearts''' (blēd′härts), ''n.'' The scarlet lychnis, ''Lychnis Chalcedonica.''

'''bleeding''' (blē′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''bleed'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A running or issuing of blood, as from the nose; a hemorrhage; the operation of letting blood, as in surgery.—'''2.''' The drawing of sap from a tree or plant.—'''3.''' In ''bookbinding'', an excessive trimming down of the margins of a book, which cuts into and mutilates the print.

'''bleeding-heart''' (blē′ding-härt), ''n.'' '''1.''' In England, a name of the wall-flower, ''Cheiranthus Cheiri.''—'''2.''' A common name of some species of ''Dicentra'', especially ''D. spectabilis'' from China, from the shape of the flowers.—'''3.''' A name sometimes applied to cultivated forms of ''Colocasia'' with colored leaves.

'''bleeding-tooth''' (blē′ding-töth), ''n.'' A common name of a shell of the family ''Neritidæ'', ''Nerita peloronta'', the toothed columella of which has

'''bleery''' (blēr′i), ''n.'' A burning brand; a fagot. Also spelled ''bleary''. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Scowder their harigals de’ils wi’ a ''bleary''.
{{right|''Hogg.''}}}}

'''bleeze'''<sup>1</sup> (blēz), ''n.'' and ''v.'' A Scotch form of ''blaze''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bleeze'''<sup>2</sup>, ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''bleezed'', ppr. ''bleezing''. To become slightly sour, as milk. [Scotch.]

'''bleik'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''a.'' See ''bleak''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bleik'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.'' See ''bleak''<sup>2</sup>.

'''blein'''†, ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''blain''.

'''bleis''', ''n. pl.'' See ''blae'', ''n.''

'''bleit'''<sup>1</sup>, '''bleit'''<sup>2</sup> (blāt), ''a.'' Same as ''blate''<sup>1</sup>, ''blate''<sup>2</sup>. [Scotch.]

'''blellum''' (blel′um), ''n.'' [Appar. imitative of senseless babble. Cf. ''blether''<sup>1</sup>.] An idle, senseless, talking, or noisy fellow. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|A blethering, blustering, drunken ''blellum''.
{{right|''Burns'', Tam o’ Shanter.}}}}

'''blench<sup>1</sup>†''' (blench), ''n.'' [< ''blench''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' A deceit; a trick.—'''2.''' A sidelong glance.
{{smaller block|These ''blenches'' gave my heart another youth.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cx.}}}}

[A variant form of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'': see ''blanch''<sup>1</sup> and ''blank.''] Upon or based upon the payment of a nominal or trifling yearly duty: applied to a sort of tenure of land: as, the estate is held ''blench'' of the crown. See ''blanch-holding.''

'''blench<sup>2</sup>''' (blench), ''v.'' [Var. of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>, partly phonetic and partly by notional confusion with ''blench''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become pale; blanch.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make white; blanch.

'''blencher''' (blen′ċhėr), ''n.'' [< ''blench''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'': see ''blancher''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1†.''' A scarecrow, or whatever frightens or turns aside or away. ''Sir T. Elyot.'' —'''2†.''' In ''hunting'', one placed where he can turn the deer from going in a particular direction; a blancher.
{{smaller block|<poem>I feel the old man’s master’d by much passion,

{{smaller block|A blethering, blustering, drunken ''blellum''.

'''blemish''' (blem′ish), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''blemisshen'', ''blemissen'' (see ''-ish''<sup>2</sup>), wound, injure, spoil, < OF. ''blemiss-'', stem of certain parts of ''blemir'', ''blesmir'' (F. ''blêmir'', grow pale, = Pr. ''blesmar'', strike, soil), < ''bleme'', ''blesme'', pale, wan; origin uncertain.]   '''1.''' To damage or impair (especially something that is well formed, or in other respects excellent); mar or make defective; destroy the perfection of; deface; sully.
{{smaller block|<poem>Vanish; or I shall give thee thy deserving,
And ''blemish'' Cæsar’s triumph.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|Sin is a soil which ''blemisheth'' the beauty of thy soul.
{{right|''R. Brathwaite.''}}}}
'''2.''' To impair morally; tarnish, as reputation or character; defame; stain: as, to ''blemish'' one’s fair fame.
{{smaller block|On a general review of the long administration of Hastings, it is impossible to deny that, against the great crimes by which it is ''blemished'', we have to set off great public services. {{right|''Macaulay'', Warren Hastings.}}}}

'''blemish''' (blem′ish), ''n.''   [< ''blemish'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A defect, flaw, or imperfection; something that mars beauty, completeness, or perfection.
{{smaller block|As he hath caused a ''blemish'' in a man, so shall it be done to him again. {{right|Lev. xxiv. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Naught had ''blemish'' there or spot,
For in that place decay was not.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 358.}}}}
'''2.''' A moral defect or injury; reproach; disgrace; that which impairs reputation; imputation.
{{smaller block|<poem>That cleare she dide from ''blemish'' criminall.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. i. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|That you have been earnest should be no ''blemish'' or discredit at all unto you. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}}

'''blemished''' (blem′isht), ''p. a.'' Having a fault or blemish; specifically, in ''her.'', broken or cut short: said of a cross, weapon, or the like, used as a bearing.

'''blemishless''' (blem′ish-les), ''a.''   [< ''blemish'', ''n.'', + ''-less''.]   Without blemish; spotless; perfect; without defect. {{smaller block|A life in all so ''blemishless.''{{right|''Feltham'', Lusoria, xxxvii.}}}}

'''blemishment''' (blem′ish-mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''blemish'', ''n.'', + ''-ment.'']   Damage; flaw; impairment.
{{smaller block|For dread of blame and honours ''blemishment.''{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. ii. 36.}}}}

'''blemmatrope''' (blem′ạ-trōp), ''n.''   [< Gr. βλέμμα, look, glance, eye (< βλέπειν, look), + τρέπειν, turn.]   An apparatus for illustrating the various positions of the eye.

'''blench<sup>1</sup>''' (blench), ''v.''   [In early mod. E. sometimes spelled ''blanch'' by confusion with ''blanch'', make white (see ''blanch''<sup>1</sup> and ''blanch''<sup>2</sup>); < ME. ''blenchen'', also ''blenken'', occasionally ''blinchen'', turn aside, evade, disconcert, usually intrans., shrink back, give way, < AS. ''blencan'' (= Icel. ''blekkja''), deceive, supposed to be a causal form of *''blincan'', blink (cf. ''drench''<sup>1</sup>, causal of ''drink''), but the latter verb does not occur in the older language: see ''blink.'' For the sense ‘deceive,’ cf. ''blear one’s eyes'', deceive, under ''blear''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To shrink; start back; give way; flinch; turn aside or fly off.
{{smaller block|Though sometimes you do ''blench'' from this to that.{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll tent him to the quick; if he but ''blench'',
I know my course.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I know his people
Are of his own choice, men that will not totter
Nor ''blench'' much at a bullet.</poem>{{right|''Fletcher'', The Pilgrim, v. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To quail: said of the eye.

'''II.'''† ''trans.'' '''1.''' To deceive; cheat.—'''2.''' To draw back from; shirk; avoid; elude; deny from fear.

{{smaller block|He now ''blenched'' what before . . . he affirmed. {{right|''Evelyn.''}}}}
'''3.''' To hinder or obstruct; disconcert; foil.
{{smaller block|The rebels besieged them, winning the even ground on the top, by carrying up great trusses of hay before them to ''blench'' the defendants’ sight and dead their shot.
{{right|''G. Carew.''}}}}

'''blench<sup>1</sup>†''' (blench), ''n.''   [< ''blench''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A deceit; a trick.—'''2.''' A sidelong glance.
{{smaller block|These ''blenches'' gave my heart another youth.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cx.}}}}

'''blench<sup>2</sup>''' (blench), ''a.'' or ''adv.''   [A variant form of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'': see ''blanch''<sup>1</sup> and ''blank.'']   Upon or based upon the payment of a nominal or trifling yearly duty: applied to a sort of tenure of land: as, the estate is held ''blench'' of the crown. See ''blanch-holding.''

'''blench<sup>2</sup>''' (blench), ''v.''   [Var. of ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>, partly phonetic and partly by notional confusion with ''blench''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become pale; blanch.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make white; blanch.

'''blencher''' (blen′ċhėr), ''n.''   [< ''blench''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'': see ''blancher''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1†.''' A scarecrow, or whatever frightens or turns aside or away.   ''Sir T. Elyot.'' —'''2†.''' In ''hunting'', one placed where he can turn the deer from going in a particular direction; a blancher.
{{smaller block|<poem>I feel the old man’s master’d by much passion,
And too high-rack’d, which makes him overshoot all
His valour should direct at, and hurt those
That stand but by as ''blenchers''.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Pilgrimage, ii. 1.}}}} '''3.''' One who blenches or flinches.

'''blench-firm†''' (blench′fėrm), ''n.'' Same as ''blanch-farm.''

'''blench-holding''' (blench′hōl″ding), ''n.'' Same as ''blanch-holding.''

'''blend<sup>1</sup>''' (blend), ''v.''; pret. ''blended,'' pp. ''blended'' or ''blent,'' ppr. ''blending.''   [< ME. ''blenden,'' mix, sometimes intrans., a secondary form of ''blanden,'' < AS. ''blandan,'' a strong verb (= OS. ''blandan'' = Icel. ''blanda'' = Sw. ''blanda'' = Dan. ''blande'' = OHG. ''blantan,'' MHG. ''blanden'' = Goth. ''blandan''), mix: see ''bland''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To mix together in such a way that the things mixed become inseparable, or cannot easily be separated.
{{smaller block|In particular: (''a'') To mix (different sorts or qualities of a commodity) in order to produce a particular brand, kind, or quality: as, to ''blend'' teas; to ''blend'' tobacco. (''b'') To mix so intimately or harmoniously that the identity or individuality of the things mixed is lost or obscured in a new product: as, many races are ''blended'' in the modern Englishman.}}
{{smaller block|Rider and horse,—friend, foe,—in one red burial ''blent.''
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Blended'' and intertwisted in this life are the sources of joys and tears.
{{right|''De Quincey.''}}}}
{{smaller block|I ''blend'' in song thy flowers and thee.
{{right|''Whittier'', First Flowers.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''c'') To cause to pass imperceptibly into one another; unite so that there shall be no perceptible line of division: as, to ''blend'' the colors of a painting.}}
'''2†.''' To mix up in the mind; confound (one thing with another).—'''3†.''' To stir up (a liquid); hence, to render turbid; figuratively, disturb.—'''4†.''' To pollute by mixture; spoil or corrupt.
{{smaller block|And all these stormes, which now his beauty ''blend.''
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, lxii.}}}}
{{smaller block|And thy throne royall with dishonour ''blent.''
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 1330.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Mix'', etc. See ''mingle.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To mix or mingle; unite intimately so as to form a harmonious whole; unite so as to be indistinguishable.
{{smaller block|<poem>And Rupert’s oath, and Cromwell’s prayer,
With battle thunder ''blended.'' {{right|''Whittier'', The Exiles.}}</poem>
<poem>Changed seemed all the fashion of the world,
And past and future into one did ''blend.''</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 349.}}}}
'''2.''' To pass imperceptibly into each other: as, sea and sky seemed to ''blend.''
{{smaller block|The distant peaks gradually ''blended'' with the white atmosphere above them. {{right|''Tyndall'', Glaciers, p. 196.}}}}
{{smaller block|It would clearly be advantageous to two varieties or incipient species if they could be kept from ''blending'', on the same principle that, when man is selecting at the same time two varieties, it is necessary that he should keep them separate. {{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, p. 246.}}}}

'''blend<sup>1</sup>''' (blend), ''n.''   [< ''blend''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A mixing or mixture, as of liquids, colors, etc.: as, tea of our own ''blend.''—'''2.''' The brand, kind, or quality produced by mixing together different sorts or qualities of a commodity: as, a fine ''blend'' of tea; the finest ''blend'' of whisky.

'''blend<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''blended'', ''blent'', ppr. ''blending.''   [< ME. ''blenden'', < AS. ''blendan'' (= OFries. ''blenda'', ''blinda'' = Dan. ''blænde'' = LG. ''blennen'' = OHG. ''blentjan'', ''blenden'', MHG. G. ''blenden''), make blind; factitive verb of ''blind'', blind: see ''blind''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' and ''v.'']   To blind; deceive.
{{smaller block|This multiplying ''blent'' [blindeth] so many oon.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 380.}}}}
{{smaller block|Reason ''blent'' through passion.{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iv. 7.}}}}

'''blendcorn''' (blend′kôrn), ''n.''   [< ''blend''<sup>1</sup> + ''corn.'' Cf. Dan. dial. ''blandekorn.'']   Wheat and rye sown and grown together.   ''N. E. D.''

'''blende''' (blend), ''n.''   [Also ''blend, blind, blinde''; < G. ''blende'', blende, < ''blenden'', blind, dazzle: see ''blend''<sup>2</sup>.]   An ore of zinc; a native sulphid of zinc, but commonly containing more or less iron, also a little cadmium, and sometimes rarer elements (gallium, indium). {{smaller|Its color is mostly brown and black, but when pure it is yellow or even white. The word ''blende'' is also employed in such compound terms as manganese-blende, zinc-blende, ruby-blende, to designate certain minerals (sulphids of the metals) characterized by a brilliant non-metallic luster. Also called ''sphalerite, false galena'', and by English miners ''mock lead'' and ''black-jack''.}}

'''blender''' (blen′dėr), ''n.'' One who or that which blends; specifically, a brush made of badgers’ hair, used by grainers and artists in blending. See ''blending''.

'''blending''' (blen′ding), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''blend''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   The act or process of combining or mingling. {{smaller|Specifically, in ''painting'': (''a'') A method of laying on different tints so that they may mingle together while wet and fuse into each other insensibly. (''b'') The process of causing pigments to melt or blend together by passing a soft brush of fitch or badgers’ hair, called a ''blender'' or ''softener'', over them with a delicate, feathery touch.}}

'''blendous''' (blen′dus), ''a.''   [< ''blende'' + ''-ous.'']   In ''mineral.'', pertaining to or consisting of blende.

'''blend-water''' (blend′wâ″tėr), ''n.'' A distemper of cattle. Also called ''more-hough''.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
